content_html_sanitized:
Posted June 13, 2005
Analysis by Richard Cowan

Last week, the San Diego Union-Tribune carried a story, “Local FBI faulted for pre-9/11 errors, FBI Office too fixed on drug investigations.”

It said, “The FBI failed to seize at least five opportunities to intercept two 9/11 hijackers before the attacks, including two instances in San Diego County when the terrorists lived with an FBI informant and were befriended by a subject of a previous FBI investigation.”

The reason, according to a report by the Justice Department's own Inspector General, “the FBI office in San Diego erred by focusing too much on drug investigations before Sept. 11, 2001.”

Of course, this was not the only instance in which such stupidity was reported. It also happened in Boston.
See
 Did The Drug War Claim Another 3,056 Casualties On 9-11? Ariana Huffington’s Extraordinary Indictment.

However, there is an irony to this story that the Union-Tribune will miss, because it has been one of the most mindlessly prohibitionist newspapers in the US. It has been “and continues to be “ as guilty as the FBI in missing the real danger to America.
See
 The San Diego Union-Tribune Poisons Its Readers. The Albany Times Union Offers An Antidote.

They are not alone in this failure. Typically, prohibitionists blame “drugs” for the problems that are actually caused by prohibition.  Other times the prohibitionist obsession with maintaining cannabis prohibition at all costs leads to an emphasis on Canada, especially “BC Bud”, because they fear the political consequences of any change in Canadian laws. One of the most bizarre examples of this nonsense was published in Time Magazine.
See
 Time Magazine Reports BC Bud 20% Less Potent Than Four Years Ago??  Incompetent Prohibitionist Propaganda and Even Worse Journalism. As Some Reporters Die to Find the Truth Others Live to Lie.

There was no mention of Mexico in that article, which is precisely the problem. Just as the FBI was obsessed with “drugs” before 9-11, focusing on Canada as a source of cannabis is missing the point entirely. It provides less than two percent of the US supply, and while prohibition related corruption in Canada is a problem, it does not begin to compare with the consequences in Mexico.

There are basically two major sources of cannabis in the US, domestic cultivation and smuggling from Mexico. Seizures at the Mexican border, the only hard data, are roughly one hundred times those at the Canadian border.
See
 As Canada Moves Toward Some Form Of Decriminalization, Canadian Narks and Walters Escalate Lying. The New Math. “Canada Replaces Mexico” As Leading Supplier of Cannabis. And If You Believe That—
and
 How Marijuana Prohibition Really Works on the Texas/Mexico Border. Contrast with the Situation at the Canadian Border. Great Journalism.

Marijuana makes up the bulk of both the physical volume of all drug seizures and of drug arrests on both borders. These arrests and seizures are a waste of time and resources that could be better spent on almost anything else, but contraband cannabis is by no means the only source of problems. Mexico is a source country for heroin as well as a conduit for South American cocaine.
See
 Now, How the Narks Created Smack in Mexico. Replacing Marijuana With Poppies. The Iron Law of Prohibition Keeps Working, But The Media Do Not

Recent reports also indicate that methamphetamine production is switching to Mexico as a result of US restrictions on ingredients, especially pseudo-ephedrine.

Last month, the Lexington (Kentucky) Herald-Leader reported that “crystal meth, a purer and deadlier version of the narcotic” (sic) is being “mass-produced in Mexican

‘super labs’ and is more potent and faster-acting than its predecessor.”

Typically, the focus of the article was about the local problem created by the crystal meth, and it ignores what this shift in production means to Mexico. Meth labs are notoriously polluting and the trade is apt to be even more violent, if that is possible.

In fact, prohibition related violence along the US/Mexico border is being compared with Baghdad, and that is not too much of an exaggeration. We hear about attacks on Iraqi police, but last week the new police chief in Nuevo Laredo was murdered only hours after he took office. (Nuevo Laredo, population 350,000, across the border from Laredo, Texas, is the busiest border crossing for trucks entering the United States from Mexico. Following NAFTA many major US companies have built plants in Mexico.)

He was the third Mexican police commander attacked in a week and the seventh killed this year in the border area. Since January, more than 60 people have been killed in just this one city. Hundreds more have been killed elsewhere in Northern Mexico. Also, Americans living along the US side of the border are complaining about the rise in both petty crime and violence, especially home robberies.

Moreover, the US is now warning tourists and others to be careful in the border area. Dozens of American citizens have been kidnapped, or have just disappeared in the border towns. When one considers how much attention is paid to the kidnapping of Westerners in Iraq, it is remarkable that no one has remarked about these abductions so much closer to home.

The US Ambassador to Mexico, Tony Garza has taken official notice: “As friends and neighbors, we should be honest with each other about the rapidly degenerating situation along the border and the near-lawlessness in some parts. The bottom line is that we simply can't allow drug traffickers to place in jeopardy the lives of our citizens and the safety of our communities.

Oh really? Welcome to the party. We should be honest with ourselves and recognize that the US drugwar is the source of this violence, which has actually increased since President Vicente Fox launched what he called the mother of all battles against the drug cartels in January. It is unfortunate that President Fox used that reference to Iraq, but to continue on that theme, it is becoming a quagmire.

There are other parallels. A group of Mexican soldiers called the Zetas have defected to join the drug gangs, and police say they are responsible for carrying out much of the Gulf Cartel’s killings. Sound familiar?

Of course, many other police are believed to be on the cartel’s payroll. There is a very long tradition, for want of a better word, of corruption in Mexico, from the highest level on down to the traffic cops. The vast sums generated by the drugwar and the violence have changed the nature of the problem. Today, the police have the choice between lead and gold to use the Colombian phrase, taking a bullet or a bribe. Think fast. 

In fairness to the Mexicans, prohibition-related official corruption is problem on both sides of the border, and in many other countries as well, but it is an added problem that Mexico simply cannot afford, and it is a threat to the US national security interests, even more than the instability in Iraq, half a world away.

Immigration and terrorism

Typical of generals who always fight the last war, the US is focusing, ineffectually, on keeping potential terrorists from entering the US via air, but we have completely lost control of the Mexican border.

Last year, over half a million illegal immigrants were arrested on the Mexico/Arizona border alone. That was about half the national total. If over a million people were stopped, certainly several million more must have gotten through.

Most of those people were simply good Mexican workers looking for an honest job in a country that badly needs their labor, but the US cannot muster the political will to provide a legal system to address our mutual needs. On the other hand, it is not hard to imagine that potential terrorists might take advantage of the situation.

US officials say they are "alarmed" that a growing number of those being stopped even come from countries such as Syria and Iran that are on the US terrorist list. In 2003, the Border Patrol arrested 39,215 so-called "OTMs," or other-than-Mexicans, along the border. In 2004, the number jumped to 65,814.

Homeland Security officials say al-Qaeda leaders want to smuggle operatives and "weapons of mass destruction" across the borders and it would seem much easier to use Mexico than to test the RCMP. James Loy, deputy secretary of the Department of Homeland Security, told Congress, Several al-Qaeda leaders believe operatives can pay their way into the country through Mexico and also believe illegal entry is more advantageous than legal entry for operational security reasons.

Ah, but we have to stop all that marijuana!

The drugwar has placed an insupportable burden on both Mexican and American law enforcement, especially but not exclusively in the border areas, that interferes with the vital national security interests of both countries. Because of the inherent weakness of the Mexican criminal justice system, the burden on Mexico is undermining the political stability of the country.

The Economist magazine reported in their June 4th issue that “according to the Mexican Interior Ministry” 97% of murders in Mexico go unpunished. In other words, the Mexican criminal justice system is incapable of providing the most basic function that citizens expect from their government.

And this is the country that we expect to bear the greatest costs of our disastrously counterproductive drugwar and maintain order along our vast border! Is it any wonder that millions of Mexicans head north?

US officials and the media still seem to have learned nothing from 9-11.
